findings.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The two statements `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger); ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` in concatenatedRSToASN1DER encode into fresh throwaway streams and discard the results. Pure dead computation on every ECDSA signature conversion; readers must determine whether these calls have a side effect (they do not), and the next maintainer editing the encoding path may 'fix' the wrong copy of the logic since the real encoding is the third ASN1Encoder two lines below.

[ADVISORY] The diff replaces the hard IllegalStateException when multiple CryptoProviders are on the classpath with a silent debug-level pick of the highest-order provider. Deployments that previously failed fast on an ambiguous classpath (e.g., both crypto/default and crypto/fips1402 jars accidentally present, both order 200) now silently select one based on ServiceLoader iteration order of ties, and the misconfiguration is only visible at debug log level; operators who relied on the startup error to detect packaging mistakes lose that signal.

[ADVISORY] readSequence() treats an indefinite-length (0x80, decoded as -1) sequence as an empty sequence and readNext() computes garbage lengths for indefinite-length elements. When length is -1 the `while (length > 0)` loop never executes, so an indefinite-length DER input silently decodes to an empty list instead of erroring, and in readNext() the `length += reset()` arithmetic on a -1 length reads tag/length bytes back as element content; callers of asn1derToConcatenatedRS then fail with 'Invalid sequence with size different to 2' or produce a corrupt signature, obscuring the real cause.

[ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default KeyStore provider (typically SUN/SunRsaSign on HotSpot), not a BouncyCastle provider. Any caller that uses this provider handle to instantiate BC-specific algorithms (as other CryptoProvider implementations' return value is used for, e.g., BouncyIntegration-style lookups) gets a JCE provider that does not implement BC algorithm names and fails with NoSuchAlgorithmException; only the ECDSA path exercised by the new test avoids this.

[ADVISORY] Roughly 15 of the 18 CryptoProvider methods throw UnsupportedOperationException with no guard or documentation distinguishing 'unsupported' from 'supported-only-in-BC providers'. Any code path that reaches this provider through the generic CryptoProvider interface (e.g., PemUtils, certificate utilities, or future authz-client features calling getAlgorithmProvider/getPemUtils) fails at runtime with UnsupportedOperationException instead of a compile-time or init-time signal; the boundary of what actually works is discoverable only by reading method bodies, which makes the next feature added to the authz client likely to hit a runtime surprise.

[BUG] getKeyStore(KeystoreUtil.KeystoreFormat format) calls KeyStore.getInstance(format.name()) with no provider, while the enum value PKCS12 maps correctly but the default BC-dependent formats relied upon elsewhere in Keycloak (e.g., BCFKS/JKS expectations in callers of this interface) resolve to the platform default provider rather than the provider this interface contract implies. A caller using this provider for a keystore format whose implementation lives only in BouncyCastle gets KeyStoreException 'no such KeyStore type' at runtime, since format.name() is passed without the BC provider that the other CryptoProvider implementations (FIPS1402Provider.getKeyStore at crypto/fips1402 line ~207) pass via BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER.

[ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER contains two dead ASN1Encoder.write() calls whose results are discarded before the real encoding is built. Two throwaway encoders are created and encoded on every ECDSA signature conversion; anyone editing this method later must reason about which write() matters, and the wasted work implies state that does not exist.

[ADVISORY] The multiple-providers condition was changed from a hard IllegalStateException to a debug-level log picking the highest-order provider, with no test covering the new selection behavior. Existing deployments that previously failed fast on an unintended second CryptoProvider on the classpath now silently select one and log at debug; a wrong provider wins invisibly and failures surface later as UnsupportedOperationException or mis-parsed signatures. The diff adds no test for the new ordering/ignore behavior.

[ADVISORY] The new provider is selected by ServiceLoader whenever it is on the classpath, but implements only the ECDSA R/S conversion — every other CryptoProvider method throws UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported yet.'). Any authz-client code path that previously relied on CryptoIntegration (JWT/JWS verification via getAlgorithmProvider, PEM handling, signature via getSignature) now gets a provider that is discoverable (order 100) and fails at operation time with a placeholder 'Not supported yet.' message instead of the prior clear 'Not able to load any cryptoProvider' error at init.

[ADVISORY] The round-trip test never verifies against Signature.verify: asn1derToConcatenatedRS output is only fed back into concatenatedRSToASN1DER, so a converter that produces consistently wrong but stable R/S bytes would pass. A corruption in integerToBytes truncation/padding logic that breaks real JWS ECDSA verification/signing interoperability (e.g. wrong-length padding) is not caught, because the test asserts only self-consistency rsConcat == rsConcat2 and never re-verifies the signature with the private key's public half.

[ADVISORY] readLength returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding (0x80), and readNext treats that -1 as a relative length (length += reset()), silently mis-parsing instead of rejecting. A malformed DER signature using indefinite-length encoding does not throw an IOException; the negative length is offset by the count of already-read bytes, producing a bogus partial read (or NegativeArraySizeException in read when the offset is 0) rather than a clean parse error for attacker-influenced signature bytes.

[ADVISORY] The out-of-bounds length check is `length >= limit`, which rejects any valid final element whose content ends exactly at the buffer end (length == limit is legal for the last TLV). A well-formed ASN.1 structure whose last component exactly fills the input is rejected with 'corrupted stream - out of bounds length found' — an edge case the ECDSA round-trip tests (random keys, short signatures) never exercise.

[ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default KeyStore's provider, not a BouncyCastle provider, so callers relying on it to obtain BC get an arbitrary JDK provider (or BC only by accident of configuration). Any code path that uses CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() to register/locate BC (e.g. BouncyIntegration-style lookups) silently operates against the wrong provider when this provider is selected, producing NoSuchAlgorithmException at call sites that assume BC is present.

[BUG] The diff silently replaces the hard failure on multiple CryptoProviders on the classpath with a debug-log-and-ignore policy, changing provider-selection semantics for every existing deployment, which is work not traceable to the stated intent of adding an authz-client crypto provider. Applications that previously failed fast with 'Multiple crypto providers loaded' (a loud classpath error) now silently pick the highest-order() provider and run with it; a wrong/unexpected provider (e.g. a test-scope provider leaking into a shaded classpath) is chosen with only a debug-level 'Ignored crypto providers' message, so misconfigured crypto goes undetected in production. This behavioral change to common/ belongs in its own change, not this PR.

[ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER contains dead code: two standalone ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger)/write(sBigInteger) invocations at lines 115-116 build encoders whose output is discarded, duplicating the work done correctly in the writeDerSeq call below. Anyone maintaining this file must reason about three encoder constructions to understand one; the next change (e.g. adding DER padding handling) risks being applied to the dead pair instead of the real one, and the wasted allocations sit on the JWT-verification hot path.

[BUG] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of the default KeyStore type (e.g. SUN/SunEC on a vanilla JDK), not a BouncyCastle provider, so any caller relying on this contract to obtain BC-backed crypto gets a non-BC provider. Code that calls CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() and passes the result as the JCE provider argument (the established contract used by server-side paths) will get Provider mismatch behavior: BC-only algorithms fail with NoSuchAlgorithmException, or operations silently execute under SUN. The provider is auto-discoverable via META-INF/services, so it can be selected globally when it is the only provider on the classpath, exposing this path outside the ECDSA-only usage it was written for.

[ADVISORY] Roughly 18 of the 20 CryptoProvider interface methods throw UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported yet.'), so this ServiceLoader-registered provider is a partial implementation that only survives if exclusively the ECDSA R/S conversion path is ever invoked through CryptoIntegration. Once the authz-client jar is on a classpath where this provider wins detection (e.g. a thin client application with no crypto/default jar), any other CryptoIntegration consumer in that application — PEM parsing, signature creation, AES ciphers, X.509 factory — throws UnsupportedOperationException at runtime instead of the NoSuchAlgorithmException-style errors callers handle; the failure mode is triggered by jar presence, not by any authz-client code path.

[ADVISORY] readLength() returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding, and readSequence()'s while (length > 0) loop then silently returns an empty list instead of rejecting the malformed DER. asn1derToConcatenatedRS receives an empty seq, throws the size!=2 IOException — so the caller gets a misleading 'Invalid sequence with size different to 2' message for a malformed/BER-encoded signature rather than a clear DER-validation error, complicating diagnosis of truncated or non-DER signature input.

[ADVISORY] The test only asserts a round-trip (rsConcat == rsConcat2) and never compares the generated DER against a known-correct ASN.1 encoding, so a symmetric encoder/decoder bug that corrupts signatures identically in both directions passes. A regression that, for example, writes r/s as raw big-endian without the ASN.1 header, or mishandles the sign byte, round-trips successfully while producing DER that real JWT verifiers reject; the suite would stay green while the client emits unverifiable ES256/384/512 signatures.

[BUG] detectProvider silently picks the highest-order provider instead of failing fast when multiple CryptoProviders are on the classpath, changing a previously thrown IllegalStateException into a debug-only log line. Deployments that previously failed fast with a clear 'Multiple crypto providers loaded' error now silently select one provider (e.g., the 100-order AuthzClientCryptoProvider over an intended server provider, or vice versa when both are present), so misconfigured classpaths produce quiet wrong-crypto behavior instead of a startup error; operators get no signal at the default log level because the notice is only debugf.

[BUG] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default KeyStore provider (e.g. SUN/SunJCE on stock JDKs), not a BouncyCastle provider, violating the CryptoProvider contract for that method. Any code path (in this library or a consumer) that calls getBouncyCastleProvider() expecting BC-specific algorithm support (BC-named algorithms, BC certificate/PEM handling) receives the JDK platform provider and fails with NoSuchAlgorithmException, or silently uses a non-BC implementation, on a plain-JVM authz-client deployment.

[ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER contains two dead ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger)/write(sBigInteger) calls whose outputs are discarded. Dead writes that can throw IOException for no effect; the next editor maintaining this method has three encoder invocations in scope where only the third one matters, increasing the chance of editing the wrong one (confusable bindings: the discarded encoders and the real one have identical shape).

[ADVISORY] readSequence() exits its loop whenever the remaining length goes <= 0 and never checks that it ended exactly at 0, so a sub-element that overruns the declared sequence length silently yields a truncated sequence. A malformed/attacker-supplied DER signature whose first element is longer than the outer sequence length parses as a 'valid' sequence without error, feeding truncated r/s material into asn1derToConcatenatedRS instead of failing; the decoder accepts encodings a strict DER decoder rejects.

[ADVISORY] order() returns 100, strictly lower than every other CryptoProvider in the codebase (200 for default/elytron/fips1402). On any classpath that also contains a server crypto module (common in embedded/test setups that pull in keycloak-core plus authz-client), CryptoIntegration.init from AuthzClient.create will select the server provider, whose ECDSACryptoProvider/getBouncyCastleProvider semantics differ from what this client was built and tested against; the ordering constant encodes no stated rationale, so the next added provider's relative priority is guesswork.

[ADVISORY] 17 of 19 CryptoProvider interface methods throw UnsupportedOperationException, making this a partial implementation registered globally via ServiceLoader with order 100. Any AuthzClient/Keycloak code path that touches CryptoIntegration for anything beyond ECDSA R/S conversion (PEM utils, AES ciphers, cert utils, signature creation) gets a runtime UnsupportedOperationException instead of a classpath-resolution error, so failures surface as UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported yet.') deep in unrelated features rather than as a missing-capability signal at provider selection time.

[ADVISORY] CryptoIntegration.init is invoked inside every AuthzClient.create() call with AuthzClient's own classloader, with no idempotence guard visible at this call site and no way for the embedder to select a different loader. Applications that construct multiple AuthzClient instances (per tenant/per config is the documented pattern) re-run provider detection each time; in OSGi or shaded-uber-jar deployments the AuthzClient classloader is the wrong one for locating consumer-registered providers, so the ServiceLoader finds nothing (IllegalStateException) or finds the wrong provider, and the embedder cannot override either behavior.

[ADVISORY] The refactor of detectProvider silently replaces the fail-fast IllegalStateException on multiple classpath providers with silent selection of the highest-order provider, changing the module's documented error contract without an explicit acceptance decision in this PR. Applications that previously failed fast at startup with a clear 'Make sure only one cryptoProvider available on the classpath' error now silently run with an arbitrary provider (e.g. AuthzClientCryptoProvider order 100 losing to DefaultCryptoProvider order 200, or winning when the default is absent); a misconfigured classpath that used to be a loud startup error becomes quietly wrong crypto behavior discovered only at runtime, and operators lose the diagnostic that named all available providers (it is now debug-level).

[ADVISORY] AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now mutates global JVM-wide crypto state (CryptoIntegration.init on the static provider singleton) as a hidden side effect of what was previously a pure factory call. Any application embedding the authz client alongside a server or another component that has already initialized CryptoIntegration gets its provider overwritten/re-detected with the authz client's classloader the first time it constructs an AuthzClient; the previously-deterministic crypto selection becomes order-of-first-AuthzClient-creation dependent, and users of other keycloak modules in the same JVM see their provider silently changed without any code they wrote changing.

[ADVISORY] A new abstract method order() is added to the public CryptoProvider interface without a default implementation, breaking compile-time compatibility for every out-of-tree CryptoProvider implementation. Third-party and downstream integrations that implement CryptoProvider (custom FIPS adapters, vendor crypto packs) stop compiling against the new keycloak-common release with 'class does not implement order()'; since the diff touches every in-tree implementer (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider, AuthzClientCryptoProvider) but ships the interface from the shared common artifact, external implementers bear a forced source break that the PR's stated intent (add an authz client provider) does not require.

[BUG] detectProvider silently selects the highest-order provider instead of failing when multiple CryptoProviders are on the classpath, downgrading a previously hard failure to a debug-level log. In a FIPS-mandated deployment where both the FIPS provider and another provider (e.g. the new authz-client provider, order 100, or default, order 200) land on the classpath, the server now silently runs with whichever provider sorts first (FIPS and default both return 200, so the pick depends on ServiceLoader order) instead of refusing to start — crypto operations may execute with a non-FIPS provider without any operator-visible error, defeating the FIPS compliance guarantee the old IllegalStateException enforced.

[ADVISORY] readLength() returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding, which callers do not handle: readNext() propagates it into read(-1) causing NegativeArraySizeException, and readSequence()'s while (length > 0) loop silently exits, accepting a truncated sequence with zero elements. An attacker-supplied DER signature (asn1derToConcatenatedRS is fed externally received JWT signatures) encoded with 0x80 indefinite length causes an uncaught RuntimeException instead of the IOException the signature path expects, and a truncated sequence decodes to garbage rather than failing — inconsistent failure behavior on untrusted crypto input.

[ADVISORY] readSequence() does not reject a sequence whose declared children consume more bytes than the declared length: length goes negative and the loop exits silently, ignoring trailing content and accepting malformed DER. A crafted ECDSA signature DER where the first INTEGER's encoded length exceeds the SEQUENCE length is 'decoded' into fewer/shorter elements and passes the size==2 check with attacker-influenced byte truncation in integerToBytes, rather than being rejected — malformed input is silently mangled instead of failing the signature path.

[ADVISORY] integerToBytes() truncates from the left (copies the last qLength bytes) when a decoded BigInteger is longer than the expected signature half-length instead of rejecting it. An oversized r or s component in an attacker-supplied DER signature is silently truncated to fit, feeding a mangled RS value into downstream verification logic rather than throwing — malformed-signature input is quietly altered instead of rejected.

[ADVISORY] CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()) inside AuthzClient.create() makes provider selection a global side effect triggered by any client construction, and the newly registered ServiceLoader entry means any application embedding the authz-client now silently has a CryptoProvider on its classpath that CryptoIntegration may select. Applications that previously had no detected provider (or relied on a deterministic single-provider error) get provider selection changed as a side effect of building an AuthzClient, and since most AuthzClientCryptoProvider methods throw UnsupportedOperationException, a deployment where this provider wins selection fails at runtime on operations (PemUtils, AES ciphers) far from the call site that caused it.

[ADVISORY] The test only verifies self-consistency (RS→DER→RS roundtrip) and never asserts the DER output against a known-good encoding, so any symmetric bug in the new ASN1Encoder/ASN1Decoder pair passes. If concatenatedRSToASN1DER emits malformed DER (e.g. wrong tag/length bytes) and asn1derToConcatenatedRS misparses it in a complementary way, Assert.assertArrayEquals(rsConcat, rsConcat2) still passes, and the broken signatures only fail at the remote verifier (e.g. the Keycloak server rejecting ES256 JWT signatures). A fixed known-answer vector (e.g. compare against BouncyCastle's ASN1 encoding for a fixed r/s pair) would pin the wire format to the spec.

[ADVISORY] The behavioral change to detectProvider (order-based selection, and demoting 'multiple providers' from IllegalStateException to a debug log) is not covered by any test in this diff. Test files checked: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java (the only test in the diff) — it exercises only AuthzClientCryptoProvider's ECDSA methods and never CryptoIntegration.detectProvider, so a regression that re-selects the wrong provider when several are on the classpath (the exact scenario the order() field was added for, e.g. authz-client 100 vs default 200) or that restores the hard exception would pass CI unnoticed.

[BUG] readSequence() silently returns a truncated or empty element list for malformed DER input: when readLength() returns -1 (indefinite-length encoding, line ~118 returns -1) the while (length > 0) loop never executes, and if a nested element's length exceeds the declared sequence length the subtraction drives length negative and the loop exits without error, so decoding 'succeeds' with dropped data. asn1derToConcatenatedRS receives a partial/empty sequence; the seq.size()!=2 check catches only some cases, but a sequence containing 2 valid INTEGERs plus trailing encoded bytes is accepted while the declared length is silently violated, so a corrupt/malformed signature can be decoded as if valid and produce a wrong concatenated R||S value that silently fails JWT signature verification downstream rather than erroring.

[ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER contains two orphaned ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger) / .write(sBigInteger) statements whose results are discarded; only the third encoder on the following lines contributes to the returned array. Wasted work on every ES256/384/512 signature conversion and a misleading impression that the standalone encoders matter; the next editor must reason about three encoders where one suffices, risking an erroneous 'fix' to the dead calls.

[ADVISORY] detectProvider previously threw IllegalStateException when multiple CryptoProviders were on the classpath; this diff replaces that hard failure with a silent pick of the highest-order provider, and since DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200, tie-breaking falls to ServiceLoader iteration order (classpath order), which is not deterministic across deployments. A server deployment that accidentally ships two crypto providers (e.g. default plus fips1402) now silently runs with an arbitrary one instead of failing fast; a FIPS-configured environment can silently end up on the non-FIPS default provider with only a debug-level log, so the misconfiguration is invisible to operators.

[ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() instantiates a full KeyStore of the default type solely to extract its Provider, and converts a KeyStoreException into an unconditional IllegalStateException; on a JVM whose default keystore type cannot be constructed (e.g. restricted FIPS environments) every crypto lookup path fails with an opaque wrapped exception naming keystore machinery for what is just a provider lookup. Failure surfaces as 'java.security.KeyStoreException' wrapped in IllegalStateException from a method contractually expected to return the BC provider, misdirecting debugging toward keystore configuration when the real issue is provider availability.

This creates a real, diff-grounded risk of runtime failures if any existing or future code uses the generic `CryptoProvider` API beyond the ECDSA conversion implementation provided here, even though the immediate diff only tests ECDSA conversion.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] getKeyStore(KeystoreUtil.KeystoreFormat format) calls KeyStore.getInstance(format.name()) with no provider, while the enum value PKCS12 maps correctly but the default BC-dependent formats relied upon elsewhere in Keycloak (e.g., BCFKS/JKS expectations in callers of this interface) resolve to the platform default provider rather than the provider this interface contract implies. A caller using this provider for a keystore format whose implementation lives only in BouncyCastle gets KeyStoreException 'no such KeyStore type' at runtime, since format.name() is passed without the BC provider that the other CryptoProvider implementations (FIPS1402Provider.getKeyStore at crypto/fips1402 line ~207) pass via BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`, `getKeyStore(KeystoreUtil.KeystoreFormat format)` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(format.name())` with no explicit provider. This differs from other `CryptoProvider` implementations shown in the diff (e.g., `FIPS1402Provider.getKeyStore` uses an explicit provider) and means keystore types that are not supported by the platform default provider will fail at runtime with `KeyStoreException`. The diff also shows `getBouncyCastleProvider()` in this provider returns the default keystore provider (not necessarily BC), reinforcing the mismatch between this provider’s purpose and its keystore instantiation behavior.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER contains two dead ASN1Encoder.write() calls whose results are discarded before the real encoding is built. Two throwaway encoders are created and encoded on every ECDSA signature conversion; anyone editing this method later must reason about which write() matters, and the wasted work implies state that does not exist.

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the lines `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` create throwaway encoders and discard them before building the actual DER sequence in the subsequent return statement. This is verifiable dead work/confusing code, but it doesn’t change the returned encoding (the real encoding is built in `writeDerSeq(...)`).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The multiple-providers condition was changed from a hard IllegalStateException to a debug-level log picking the highest-order provider, with no test covering the new selection behavior. Existing deployments that previously failed fast on an unintended second CryptoProvider on the classpath now silently select one and log at debug; a wrong provider wins invisibly and failures surface later as UnsupportedOperationException or mis-parsed signatures. The diff adds no test for the new ordering/ignore behavior.

adjudication.rationale: The diff in `common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java` changes behavior from throwing `IllegalStateException` on multiple `CryptoProvider`s to sorting by the new `CryptoProvider::order` (descending) and silently selecting the first while only logging ignored providers at debug. This is a significant behavioral change and there is no test added in the diff that exercises/guards the new ordering/selection and ignore behavior (the only new test, `ECDSAAlgorithmTest`, covers ECDSA signature conversion, not provider selection).

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new provider is selected by ServiceLoader whenever it is on the classpath, but implements only the ECDSA R/S conversion — every other CryptoProvider method throws UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported yet.'). Any authz-client code path that previously relied on CryptoIntegration (JWT/JWS verification via getAlgorithmProvider, PEM handling, signature via getSignature) now gets a provider that is discoverable (order 100) and fails at operation time with a placeholder 'Not supported yet.' message instead of the prior clear 'Not able to load any cryptoProvider' error at init.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds AuthzClientCryptoProvider registered via ServiceLoader, but CryptoIntegration.detectProvider() now sorts providers by CryptoProvider::order descending. AuthzClientCryptoProvider.order() returns 100, while existing providers (DefaultCryptoProvider/WildFlyElytronProvider/FIPS1402Provider) are updated to return 200, so the new provider is *not* selected when those are present. The finding’s claim that it will be selected “whenever it is on the classpath” due to order 100 is contradicted by the diff. While many methods in AuthzClientCryptoProvider throw UnsupportedOperationException, the finding’s broader claim that authz-client paths relying on getAlgorithmProvider/PEM/getSignature will now fail is not shown in this diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The round-trip test never verifies against Signature.verify: asn1derToConcatenatedRS output is only fed back into concatenatedRSToASN1DER, so a converter that produces consistently wrong but stable R/S bytes would pass. A corruption in integerToBytes truncation/padding logic that breaks real JWS ECDSA verification/signing interoperability (e.g. wrong-length padding) is not caught, because the test asserts only self-consistency rsConcat == rsConcat2 and never re-verifies the signature with the private key's public half.

adjudication.rationale: The new test `ECDSAAlgorithmTest` only checks converter self-consistency: it converts a real DER signature to concatenated R/S (`asn1derToConcatenatedRS`), converts back (`concatenatedRSToASN1DER`), then converts again and asserts `rsConcat == rsConcat2`. It never calls `Signature.verify(...)` with `keyPair.getPublic()` (or otherwise verifies that the reconstructed DER signature is actually valid for the signed data). Therefore, a stable-but-wrong conversion (e.g., due to padding/truncation behavior in `integerToBytes` inside `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`) could still pass this test, making the finding a concrete, diff-grounded test-gap rather than a proven functional defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] readLength returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding (0x80), and readNext treats that -1 as a relative length (length += reset()), silently mis-parsing instead of rejecting. A malformed DER signature using indefinite-length encoding does not throw an IOException; the negative length is offset by the count of already-read bytes, producing a bogus partial read (or NegativeArraySizeException in read when the offset is 0) rather than a clean parse error for attacker-influenced signature bytes.
matched_golden_ids: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both describe the same underlying bug: indefinite-length encoding yields length = -1, and subsequent arithmetic that adjusts length by the number of bytes already read (e.g., subtracting/adding bytes.length/reset count) turns the sentinel -1 into a misleading non-error value. This causes incorrect parsing/processing instead of rejecting indefinite-length encodings.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The out-of-bounds length check is `length >= limit`, which rejects any valid final element whose content ends exactly at the buffer end (length == limit is legal for the last TLV). A well-formed ASN.1 structure whose last component exactly fills the input is rejected with 'corrupted stream - out of bounds length found' — an edge case the ECDSA round-trip tests (random keys, short signatures) never exercise.

adjudication.rationale: In ASN1Decoder.readLength(), the `length >= limit` check is only applied for long-form lengths (`if (length > 127)`). `readLength()` returns the *content* length (per DER), while `limit` is the total size of the byte array including tag/length bytes. For any well-formed TLV parsed by this decoder (e.g., via `readInteger()` / `readNext()`), the content length cannot legally equal the total buffer length because the tag+length header consumes at least 2 bytes. So the specific claim that a valid final TLV with `length == limit` would be rejected is not supported by the diff’s code paths.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider returns the default KeyStore's provider, not a BouncyCastle provider, so callers relying on it to obtain BC get an arbitrary JDK provider (or BC only by accident of configuration). Any code path that uses CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() to register/locate BC (e.g. BouncyIntegration-style lookups) silently operates against the wrong provider when this provider is selected, producing NoSuchAlgorithmException at call sites that assume BC is present.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new service-loaded `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` (via `META-INF/services/...CryptoProvider`) and makes `AuthzClient.create(...)` call `CryptoIntegration.init(...)`, meaning this provider can be selected at runtime. In that provider, `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which is not guaranteed to be a BouncyCastle provider and is effectively an arbitrary JDK provider. However, from the diff alone we cannot verify any concrete code path in this PR that actually uses `CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider()` to perform BC-specific lookups/registration and would therefore throw `NoSuchAlgorithmException`—the provider also leaves many other methods as `UnsupportedOperationException`, suggesting it may be intended as a minimal implementation for authz-client. So the concern is real and diff-grounded (misleading/incorrect contract fulfillment), but the claimed broken behavior at call sites is not directly demonstrable from the shown changes.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The diff silently replaces the hard failure on multiple CryptoProviders on the classpath with a debug-log-and-ignore policy, changing provider-selection semantics for every existing deployment, which is work not traceable to the stated intent of adding an authz-client crypto provider. Applications that previously failed fast with 'Multiple crypto providers loaded' (a loud classpath error) now silently pick the highest-order() provider and run with it; a wrong/unexpected provider (e.g. a test-scope provider leaking into a shaded classpath) is chosen with only a debug-level 'Ignored crypto providers' message, so misconfigured crypto goes undetected in production. This behavioral change to common/ belongs in its own change, not this PR.

adjudication.rationale: The diff in `common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java` changes `detectProvider(...)` from throwing an `IllegalStateException` when `foundProviders.size() > 1` to sorting providers by the new `CryptoProvider::order` (added in `CryptoProvider`) and selecting the highest-order provider while only debug-logging the rest. This is a verifiable, global provider-selection semantics change in `common/` that goes beyond “adding an authz-client crypto provider” and can hide classpath misconfiguration that previously failed fast. However, the diff does not prove the new behavior is incorrect in itself (it may be intentional), so it’s better classified as a scope/architecture concern rather than a definite defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER contains dead code: two standalone ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger)/write(sBigInteger) invocations at lines 115-116 build encoders whose output is discarded, duplicating the work done correctly in the writeDerSeq call below. Anyone maintaining this file must reason about three encoder constructions to understand one; the next change (e.g. adding DER padding handling) risks being applied to the dead pair instead of the real one, and the wasted allocations sit on the JWT-verification hot path.

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, there are two standalone calls `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` whose returned encoders/byte output are never used. The method then correctly constructs the DER sequence using new encoders in `writeDerSeq(...)`. The first two calls therefore duplicate work/allocations and add maintenance confusion, but they do not change the returned value or introduce an observable functional defect in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the provider of the default KeyStore type (e.g. SUN/SunEC on a vanilla JDK), not a BouncyCastle provider, so any caller relying on this contract to obtain BC-backed crypto gets a non-BC provider. Code that calls CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider() and passes the result as the JCE provider argument (the established contract used by server-side paths) will get Provider mismatch behavior: BC-only algorithms fail with NoSuchAlgorithmException, or operations silently execute under SUN. The provider is auto-discoverable via META-INF/services, so it can be selected globally when it is the only provider on the classpath, exposing this path outside the ECDSA-only usage it was written for.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`, `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()` (see `AuthzClientCryptoProvider#getBouncyCastleProvider`). That provider is the JDK keystore provider (often `SUN`), not BouncyCastle, which contradicts the `CryptoProvider#getBouncyCastleProvider()` contract/name and can cause provider-mismatch failures if callers pass it as the JCE provider for BC-dependent operations. This risk is amplified because the provider is made globally discoverable via `META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider`, and `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` now selects a provider (highest `order()`) instead of failing on multiples; if this is the only provider on the classpath, it will be selected and expose the incorrect provider return value outside the intended ECDSA-only use.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] Roughly 18 of the 20 CryptoProvider interface methods throw UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported yet.'), so this ServiceLoader-registered provider is a partial implementation that only survives if exclusively the ECDSA R/S conversion path is ever invoked through CryptoIntegration. Once the authz-client jar is on a classpath where this provider wins detection (e.g. a thin client application with no crypto/default jar), any other CryptoIntegration consumer in that application — PEM parsing, signature creation, AES ciphers, X.509 factory — throws UnsupportedOperationException at runtime instead of the NoSuchAlgorithmException-style errors callers handle; the failure mode is triggered by jar presence, not by any authz-client code path.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a ServiceLoader-registered CryptoProvider (META-INF/services/... -> AuthzClientCryptoProvider) where most interface methods intentionally throw UnsupportedOperationException, while only ECDSA R/S conversion is implemented. CryptoIntegration.detectProvider was changed to pick the highest-order provider and no longer fail when multiple are present; AuthzClient.create() now calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()). In an application where authz-client is the only jar contributing a CryptoProvider, CryptoIntegration will detect this partial provider and later calls to other CryptoIntegration functionality (PEM/cert utilities, ciphers, signatures, etc.) would throw at runtime. This is a concrete, diff-grounded integration/architecture risk, though the claim about callers specifically expecting NoSuchAlgorithmException cannot be verified from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] readLength() returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding, and readSequence()'s while (length > 0) loop then silently returns an empty list instead of rejecting the malformed DER. asn1derToConcatenatedRS receives an empty seq, throws the size!=2 IOException — so the caller gets a misleading 'Invalid sequence with size different to 2' message for a malformed/BER-encoded signature rather than a clear DER-validation error, complicating diagnosis of truncated or non-DER signature input.

adjudication.rationale: In ASN1Decoder.readLength(), a length byte of 0x80 returns -1 (indefinite-length). readSequence() then does `while (length > 0)` and will return an empty `List<byte[]>` instead of rejecting the non-DER/BER indefinite-length encoding. Downstream, asn1derToConcatenatedRS() checks `seq.size() != 2` and throws `IOException("Invalid sequence with size different to 2")`, which is indeed a misleading error for this malformed/BER input path. The diff shows no explicit rejection of `length == -1` in readSequence().

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The test only asserts a round-trip (rsConcat == rsConcat2) and never compares the generated DER against a known-correct ASN.1 encoding, so a symmetric encoder/decoder bug that corrupts signatures identically in both directions passes. A regression that, for example, writes r/s as raw big-endian without the ASN.1 header, or mishandles the sign byte, round-trips successfully while producing DER that real JWT verifiers reject; the suite would stay green while the client emits unverifiable ES256/384/512 signatures.

adjudication.rationale: The added ECDSAAlgorithmTest only checks a round-trip property: it converts a real JCA DER signature to concatenated R||S and back to DER, then back again, and asserts rsConcat == rsConcat2 (see ECDSAAlgorithmTest.test()). It never validates that the produced DER (asn1Des) is correct/standard (e.g., by verifying the signature with JCA using asn1Des, or comparing against a known-good DER encoding). Therefore, a symmetric bug in ASN1Decoder/ASN1Encoder or in the conversion logic inside AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider() could still pass this test while emitting DER that external verifiers reject.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] detectProvider silently picks the highest-order provider instead of failing fast when multiple CryptoProviders are on the classpath, changing a previously thrown IllegalStateException into a debug-only log line. Deployments that previously failed fast with a clear 'Multiple crypto providers loaded' error now silently select one provider (e.g., the 100-order AuthzClientCryptoProvider over an intended server provider, or vice versa when both are present), so misconfigured classpaths produce quiet wrong-crypto behavior instead of a startup error; operators get no signal at the default log level because the notice is only debugf.

adjudication.rationale: The diff explicitly changes `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` to sort providers by `CryptoProvider::order` and return the highest-order one, whereas it previously threw `IllegalStateException` when `foundProviders.size() > 1` (that exception block is removed). The new behavior only emits a `logger.debugf("Ignored crypto providers: ...")` message when more than one provider is present. This is a real, diff-grounded behavioral/operational concern (silent selection + debug-only notice), but it appears to be an intentional design change enabled by the newly added `CryptoProvider.order()` API rather than a clearly unintended defect.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default KeyStore provider (e.g. SUN/SunJCE on stock JDKs), not a BouncyCastle provider, violating the CryptoProvider contract for that method. Any code path (in this library or a consumer) that calls getBouncyCastleProvider() expecting BC-specific algorithm support (BC-named algorithms, BC certificate/PEM handling) receives the JDK platform provider and fails with NoSuchAlgorithmException, or silently uses a non-BC implementation, on a plain-JVM authz-client deployment.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` implementing `CryptoProvider`. Its `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, i.e., the JDK default KeyStore provider (commonly `SUN`), not a BouncyCastle provider. This conflicts with the `CryptoProvider` method contract/comment (“Get bouncycastle provider”) and could break callers expecting BC-specific algorithms/behavior. The issue is directly visible in the added implementation.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER contains two dead ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger)/write(sBigInteger) calls whose outputs are discarded. Dead writes that can throw IOException for no effect; the next editor maintaining this method has three encoder invocations in scope where only the third one matters, increasing the chance of editing the wrong one (confusable bindings: the discarded encoders and the real one have identical shape).

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, there are two standalone calls `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` whose returned encoders/bytes are never used. The actual returned value is produced by a separate third encoder invocation in the subsequent `return ASN1Encoder.create().writeDerSeq(...).toByteArray();`. These first two calls are dead/confusing and can (per signature) throw IOException without affecting output, creating maintainability risk, but they do not change the method’s functional result given the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] readSequence() exits its loop whenever the remaining length goes <= 0 and never checks that it ended exactly at 0, so a sub-element that overruns the declared sequence length silently yields a truncated sequence. A malformed/attacker-supplied DER signature whose first element is longer than the outer sequence length parses as a 'valid' sequence without error, feeding truncated r/s material into asn1derToConcatenatedRS instead of failing; the decoder accepts encodings a strict DER decoder rejects.

adjudication.rationale: In ASN1Decoder.readSequence(), the loop condition is `while (length > 0)` and it subtracts `bytes.length` after each `readNext()`. If a child element’s encoded length exceeds the remaining declared SEQUENCE length, `length` becomes negative and the loop exits without any validation that it ended exactly at 0. There is no subsequent check (e.g., `if (length != 0) throw ...`) to detect overrun/malformed DER, so non-strict encodings can be accepted rather than rejected, matching the finding’s claim about silently truncating/accepting invalid sequences.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] order() returns 100, strictly lower than every other CryptoProvider in the codebase (200 for default/elytron/fips1402). On any classpath that also contains a server crypto module (common in embedded/test setups that pull in keycloak-core plus authz-client), CryptoIntegration.init from AuthzClient.create will select the server provider, whose ECDSACryptoProvider/getBouncyCastleProvider semantics differ from what this client was built and tested against; the ordering constant encodes no stated rationale, so the next added provider's relative priority is guesswork.

adjudication.rationale: The diff makes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider sort CryptoProvider implementations by descending order() and select the first one. In the same diff, AuthzClient.create() calls CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()), and the newly added AuthzClientCryptoProvider returns order()=100 while DefaultCryptoProvider/WildFlyElytronProvider/FIPS1402Provider return 200. Therefore, when multiple providers are on the classpath, the authz-client provider will be ignored in favor of a 200-order provider. Whether that causes incorrect behavior (e.g., differing ECDSA semantics) isn’t verifiable from the diff alone, but the ordering choice is real and creates an architecture/priority ambiguity for this new provider.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] 17 of 19 CryptoProvider interface methods throw UnsupportedOperationException, making this a partial implementation registered globally via ServiceLoader with order 100. Any AuthzClient/Keycloak code path that touches CryptoIntegration for anything beyond ECDSA R/S conversion (PEM utils, AES ciphers, cert utils, signature creation) gets a runtime UnsupportedOperationException instead of a classpath-resolution error, so failures surface as UnsupportedOperationException('Not supported yet.') deep in unrelated features rather than as a missing-capability signal at provider selection time.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` that implements `CryptoProvider` but most methods explicitly throw `UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.")` (e.g., `getPemUtils`, `getCertificateUtils`, `getAesCbcCipher`, `getSignature`, etc.). It is registered via `META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider`, and `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` now calls `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())`, which will cause this provider to be discoverable/selected when no higher-order provider is present. While the diff doesn't show an immediate call path that uses the unsupported methods, the registration + partial implementation makes future/other code paths that rely on `CryptoIntegration.getProvider()` brittle and fail at runtime with UOE rather than failing earlier at provider selection.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] CryptoIntegration.init is invoked inside every AuthzClient.create() call with AuthzClient's own classloader, with no idempotence guard visible at this call site and no way for the embedder to select a different loader. Applications that construct multiple AuthzClient instances (per tenant/per config is the documented pattern) re-run provider detection each time; in OSGi or shaded-uber-jar deployments the AuthzClient classloader is the wrong one for locating consumer-registered providers, so the ServiceLoader finds nothing (IllegalStateException) or finds the wrong provider, and the embedder cannot override either behavior.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader());` directly inside `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` (authz/client/src/main/java/.../AuthzClient.java), hard-wiring the classloader used for `ServiceLoader.load(CryptoProvider.class, classLoader)` in `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` (common/src/main/java/.../CryptoIntegration.java). From the diff, there is no call-site guard to prevent repeated init on multiple `AuthzClient.create(...)` calls, and no API shown here to let embedders supply an alternate classloader. While the downstream impact (re-running detection, OSGi/shaded classloader mismatch, inability to override) is plausible given the `ServiceLoader` usage, whether it is an actual defect depends on unseen `CryptoIntegration.init` idempotence/caching behavior and deployment specifics not shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The refactor of detectProvider silently replaces the fail-fast IllegalStateException on multiple classpath providers with silent selection of the highest-order provider, changing the module's documented error contract without an explicit acceptance decision in this PR. Applications that previously failed fast at startup with a clear 'Make sure only one cryptoProvider available on the classpath' error now silently run with an arbitrary provider (e.g. AuthzClientCryptoProvider order 100 losing to DefaultCryptoProvider order 200, or winning when the default is absent); a misconfigured classpath that used to be a loud startup error becomes quietly wrong crypto behavior discovered only at runtime, and operators lose the diagnostic that named all available providers (it is now debug-level).

adjudication.rationale: The diff in common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java removes the previous fail-fast IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider is discovered. It now sorts providers by CryptoProvider::order (new method added in CryptoProvider.java) and returns the highest-order provider, only logging ignored providers at debug level. This is a concrete, diff-grounded behavior/diagnostic-contract change (e.g., DefaultCryptoProvider/WildFlyElytronProvider/FIPS1402Provider now report order()=200 while the newly added AuthzClientCryptoProvider returns 100), but it’s not inherently a correctness defect by itself—rather an explicit policy change that may warrant an acceptance decision and/or documentation/log-level discussion.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now mutates global JVM-wide crypto state (CryptoIntegration.init on the static provider singleton) as a hidden side effect of what was previously a pure factory call. Any application embedding the authz client alongside a server or another component that has already initialized CryptoIntegration gets its provider overwritten/re-detected with the authz client's classloader the first time it constructs an AuthzClient; the previously-deterministic crypto selection becomes order-of-first-AuthzClient-creation dependent, and users of other keycloak modules in the same JVM see their provider silently changed without any code they wrote changing.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a new side effect in `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` by calling `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader());` before constructing the client. `CryptoIntegration` is a global/static integration point (it discovers `CryptoProvider` via `ServiceLoader` and now selects one by `order()`), so initializing it from this factory method is an architecture/scope concern that can affect crypto provider selection beyond the authz client. However, the finding’s stronger claim that it will overwrite an already-initialized provider / become order-of-first-AuthzClient-creation dependent cannot be fully verified from the diff because `CryptoIntegration.init(...)` implementation and whether it is idempotent are not shown here.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] A new abstract method order() is added to the public CryptoProvider interface without a default implementation, breaking compile-time compatibility for every out-of-tree CryptoProvider implementation. Third-party and downstream integrations that implement CryptoProvider (custom FIPS adapters, vendor crypto packs) stop compiling against the new keycloak-common release with 'class does not implement order()'; since the diff touches every in-tree implementer (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider, AuthzClientCryptoProvider) but ships the interface from the shared common artifact, external implementers bear a forced source break that the PR's stated intent (add an authz client provider) does not require.
matched_golden_ids: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
adjudication_records.primary_judge_reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue point out that adding a new abstract order() method to the public CryptoProvider interface will break backward/source compatibility for existing third-party implementations that must now implement the new method to compile.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] detectProvider silently selects the highest-order provider instead of failing when multiple CryptoProviders are on the classpath, downgrading a previously hard failure to a debug-level log. In a FIPS-mandated deployment where both the FIPS provider and another provider (e.g. the new authz-client provider, order 100, or default, order 200) land on the classpath, the server now silently runs with whichever provider sorts first (FIPS and default both return 200, so the pick depends on ServiceLoader order) instead of refusing to start — crypto operations may execute with a non-FIPS provider without any operator-visible error, defeating the FIPS compliance guarantee the old IllegalStateException enforced.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider: it now collects providers from ServiceLoader, sorts them by CryptoProvider::order descending, and always returns the first provider, only logging (at debug) any additional providers. The prior behavior (throwing IllegalStateException when foundProviders.size() > 1) has been removed. Since multiple built-in providers now all return the same order (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider each return 200), selection among them becomes dependent on ServiceLoader order for ties, and the presence of multiple providers no longer fails fast or produces an operator-visible error. This matches the finding’s claim that a previously hard failure is now a silent selection that can pick an unintended provider when multiple are on the classpath.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] readLength() returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding, which callers do not handle: readNext() propagates it into read(-1) causing NegativeArraySizeException, and readSequence()'s while (length > 0) loop silently exits, accepting a truncated sequence with zero elements. An attacker-supplied DER signature (asn1derToConcatenatedRS is fed externally received JWT signatures) encoded with 0x80 indefinite length causes an uncaught RuntimeException instead of the IOException the signature path expects, and a truncated sequence decodes to garbage rather than failing — inconsistent failure behavior on untrusted crypto input.

adjudication.rationale: In the new ASN1Decoder, readLength() explicitly returns -1 for indefinite-length encoding (0x80). Callers don’t handle this safely: readSequence() uses `while (length > 0)` so an indefinite-length SEQUENCE returns an empty list without consuming content, and readInteger() passes the returned length directly into `read(length)`, which will attempt `new byte[-1]` and throw NegativeArraySizeException (a runtime exception) instead of IOException. This is reachable from untrusted DER input via AuthzClientCryptoProvider.ECDSACryptoProvider.asn1derToConcatenatedRS(), which decodes externally supplied ECDSA signatures.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] readSequence() does not reject a sequence whose declared children consume more bytes than the declared length: length goes negative and the loop exits silently, ignoring trailing content and accepting malformed DER. A crafted ECDSA signature DER where the first INTEGER's encoded length exceeds the SEQUENCE length is 'decoded' into fewer/shorter elements and passes the size==2 check with attacker-influenced byte truncation in integerToBytes, rather than being rejected — malformed input is silently mangled instead of failing the signature path.

adjudication.rationale: In ASN1Decoder.readSequence(), the declared SEQUENCE length is read into `length`, then the loop subtracts the actual encoded child size (`bytes.length`) after each `readNext()`. If the encoded children consume more bytes than the SEQUENCE’s declared length, `length` becomes negative and the loop exits without any exception, returning whatever elements were read. There is no check that the total consumed bytes equals the declared SEQUENCE length (or that `length` never goes below 0). This means malformed DER with inconsistent length fields can be accepted and parsed (e.g., two INTEGER encodings whose total length exceeds the SEQUENCE length), which is exactly what the finding describes as “silently mangled instead of failing.”

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] integerToBytes() truncates from the left (copies the last qLength bytes) when a decoded BigInteger is longer than the expected signature half-length instead of rejecting it. An oversized r or s component in an attacker-supplied DER signature is silently truncated to fit, feeding a mangled RS value into downstream verification logic rather than throwing — malformed-signature input is quietly altered instead of rejected.

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider#getEcdsaCryptoProvider(), integerToBytes(BigInteger s, int qLength) explicitly truncates when s.toByteArray().length > qLength by copying only the last qLength bytes (dropping the most-significant bytes) instead of rejecting the value. This is reachable from asn1derToConcatenatedRS(), which decodes attacker-controlled DER integers for r and s via ASN1Decoder.readInteger(). As a result, oversized r/s components are silently altered to a different value rather than treated as invalid/malformed, matching the finding.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader()) inside AuthzClient.create() makes provider selection a global side effect triggered by any client construction, and the newly registered ServiceLoader entry means any application embedding the authz-client now silently has a CryptoProvider on its classpath that CryptoIntegration may select. Applications that previously had no detected provider (or relied on a deterministic single-provider error) get provider selection changed as a side effect of building an AuthzClient, and since most AuthzClientCryptoProvider methods throw UnsupportedOperationException, a deployment where this provider wins selection fails at runtime on operations (PemUtils, AES ciphers) far from the call site that caused it.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a global initialization side effect by calling `CryptoIntegration.init(AuthzClient.class.getClassLoader())` inside `AuthzClient.create(Configuration)` (authz/client/src/main/java/.../AuthzClient.java). It also registers a new `CryptoProvider` via `META-INF/services/org.keycloak.common.crypto.CryptoProvider`, making `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` discoverable by `ServiceLoader`. `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` was changed to no longer fail when multiple providers are present, but instead to sort by `CryptoProvider::order` and pick the highest (common/src/main/java/.../CryptoIntegration.java + CryptoProvider.java). If an application embeds authz-client without another crypto module on the classpath, this new provider (order=100) becomes the selected global provider, yet most of its required methods throw `UnsupportedOperationException` (e.g., `getPemUtils`, `getCertificateUtils`, `getAesCbcCipher`, `getAesGcmCipher`, etc. in AuthzClientCryptoProvider). That creates a real runtime-failure mode introduced by this diff, potentially far from the AuthzClient construction that triggered init.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The test only verifies self-consistency (RS→DER→RS roundtrip) and never asserts the DER output against a known-good encoding, so any symmetric bug in the new ASN1Encoder/ASN1Decoder pair passes. If concatenatedRSToASN1DER emits malformed DER (e.g. wrong tag/length bytes) and asn1derToConcatenatedRS misparses it in a complementary way, Assert.assertArrayEquals(rsConcat, rsConcat2) still passes, and the broken signatures only fail at the remote verifier (e.g. the Keycloak server rejecting ES256 JWT signatures). A fixed known-answer vector (e.g. compare against BouncyCastle's ASN1 encoding for a fixed r/s pair) would pin the wire format to the spec.

adjudication.rationale: The new test `ECDSAAlgorithmTest` only asserts a roundtrip property using the same `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` ASN.1 encoder/decoder (`asn1derToConcatenatedRS` -> `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` -> `asn1derToConcatenatedRS`, then `Assert.assertArrayEquals`). It does not assert that the DER produced by `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` matches a known-good DER encoding (e.g., from a standard ASN.1 library) for fixed r/s inputs. While the test does exercise parsing of a real JCA-produced DER signature (`Signature.sign()`), it still wouldn’t catch an encoder that emits non-compliant DER as long as this decoder can read it back. This is a test-quality gap rather than a verifiable functional defect in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The behavioral change to detectProvider (order-based selection, and demoting 'multiple providers' from IllegalStateException to a debug log) is not covered by any test in this diff. Test files checked: authz/client/src/test/java/org/keycloak/authorization/client/test/ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java (the only test in the diff) — it exercises only AuthzClientCryptoProvider's ECDSA methods and never CryptoIntegration.detectProvider, so a regression that re-selects the wrong provider when several are on the classpath (the exact scenario the order() field was added for, e.g. authz-client 100 vs default 200) or that restores the hard exception would pass CI unnoticed.

adjudication.rationale: The diff changes CryptoIntegration.detectProvider to sort ServiceLoader results by CryptoProvider::order (reversed) and no longer throws when multiple providers are present; instead it picks the first and logs the rest (common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java). The only added test (authz/client/src/test/java/.../ECDSAAlgorithmTest.java) instantiates AuthzClientCryptoProvider directly and exercises only ECDSA ASN.1 conversion; it never calls CryptoIntegration.init/getProvider nor covers the multi-provider selection/"no longer throw" behavior that order() was introduced for (authz-client provider order=100 vs default providers order=200). Thus the review concern (new nontrivial selection behavior lacks test coverage) is specific and grounded in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] readSequence() silently returns a truncated or empty element list for malformed DER input: when readLength() returns -1 (indefinite-length encoding, line ~118 returns -1) the while (length > 0) loop never executes, and if a nested element's length exceeds the declared sequence length the subtraction drives length negative and the loop exits without error, so decoding 'succeeds' with dropped data. asn1derToConcatenatedRS receives a partial/empty sequence; the seq.size()!=2 check catches only some cases, but a sequence containing 2 valid INTEGERs plus trailing encoded bytes is accepted while the declared length is silently violated, so a corrupt/malformed signature can be decoded as if valid and produce a wrong concatenated R||S value that silently fails JWT signature verification downstream rather than erroring.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `ASN1Decoder.readSequence()`, `int length = readLength();` can be `-1` for indefinite-length encoding (see `readLength()` returning `-1` when `length == 0x80`). The subsequent `while (length > 0)` then never runs, returning an empty list without error. Also, `length = length - bytes.length;` will go negative if an element’s encoded length exceeds the declared sequence length, and the loop exits without detecting the violation, returning a truncated element list. This behavior is directly visible in the diff and can allow malformed ASN.1/DER inputs to be accepted/partially decoded instead of failing.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] concatenatedRSToASN1DER contains two orphaned ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger) / .write(sBigInteger) statements whose results are discarded; only the third encoder on the following lines contributes to the returned array. Wasted work on every ES256/384/512 signature conversion and a misleading impression that the standalone encoders matter; the next editor must reason about three encoders where one suffices, risking an erroneous 'fix' to the dead calls.

adjudication.rationale: In AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getEcdsaCryptoProvider().concatenatedRSToASN1DER, the lines `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);` create encoders, write into them, and then discard them. Only the later `ASN1Encoder.create().writeDerSeq(ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger), ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger)).toByteArray()` contributes to the returned DER. This is wasted work and potentially confusing, but it does not change the returned value or break functionality as shown in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] detectProvider previously threw IllegalStateException when multiple CryptoProviders were on the classpath; this diff replaces that hard failure with a silent pick of the highest-order provider, and since DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider and FIPS1402Provider all return order() == 200, tie-breaking falls to ServiceLoader iteration order (classpath order), which is not deterministic across deployments. A server deployment that accidentally ships two crypto providers (e.g. default plus fips1402) now silently runs with an arbitrary one instead of failing fast; a FIPS-configured environment can silently end up on the non-FIPS default provider with only a debug-level log, so the misconfiguration is invisible to operators.

adjudication.rationale: In common/src/main/java/org/keycloak/common/crypto/CryptoIntegration.java, detectProvider() now sorts providers by CryptoProvider::order (descending) and returns the first, only logging ignored providers at debug level, whereas it previously threw IllegalStateException when foundProviders.size() > 1. In this diff, DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all implement order() returning 200, so when more than one is present the comparator ties and the chosen provider depends on ServiceLoader iteration/encounter order (classpath-dependent). That makes provider selection non-deterministic across deployments and can silently select an unintended provider (e.g., non-FIPS) without an operator-visible failure.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] getBouncyCastleProvider() instantiates a full KeyStore of the default type solely to extract its Provider, and converts a KeyStoreException into an unconditional IllegalStateException; on a JVM whose default keystore type cannot be constructed (e.g. restricted FIPS environments) every crypto lookup path fails with an opaque wrapped exception naming keystore machinery for what is just a provider lookup. Failure surfaces as 'java.security.KeyStoreException' wrapped in IllegalStateException from a method contractually expected to return the BC provider, misdirecting debugging toward keystore configuration when the real issue is provider availability.

adjudication.rationale: In the newly added `AuthzClientCryptoProvider`, `getBouncyCastleProvider()` is implemented as `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()` and wraps `KeyStoreException` in `IllegalStateException` (see `AuthzClientCryptoProvider#getBouncyCastleProvider`). This both (a) does not actually return a BouncyCastle provider as the `CryptoProvider` contract implies, and (b) can fail purely due to keystore construction issues, causing crypto provider selection/usage to fail with a misleading keystore-related exception even though the intent is provider lookup.
